blocks.text: …the path to composure

Long-line training is a long-term, everyday-compatible learning process for our dog and ourselves. On the one hand it forms the basis for a relaxed time together in all everyday situations on the move, and on the other hand it can significantly and positively shape and deepen the teamwork between handler and dog.

Long-line training is a form of long-term and therefore profound conditioning. It ensures that our dog moves reliably and without stress within our sphere of influence and, later, depending on training progress, also lets us lead it reliably in off-leash work.
Long-line training is essential for sustainable dog training.
Leash and training environment 🦮
Principle: The longer-term and more varied the long-line training is practised, the safer and more reliably we can later be out with our dog off the leash.

Leash length: We always train with a leash of 6 to a maximum of 10 metres in length. The leash should be easy to grip but not too heavy. Be careful with thin leashes – they carry a high risk of injury for everyone involved.

Recommendation: Since leashes are subject to constant wear, we recommend flat webbing sold by the metre from a DIY store. Together with a sturdy carabiner and a small knot at the end (no loop!), this makes the ideal training leash for little money.

Training environment: The first training sessions take place without notable distraction in open terrain, far from hazardous environmental conditions. As training progresses, we apply the training with increasing distraction – but always only in situations that allow a successful outcome.
Step 1: Addressing the dog 🗣️

Whenever our dog wants to use up the full radius of the long leash while walking, we address it by name in a calm and friendly tone of voice and stop at the same time. We may add a short, light leash signal.

It is important that, on the one hand, the leash was not yet taut and, on the other hand, that our calm manner does not trigger any state of alarm that the dog could then mistakenly interpret as something outside. The dog should now turn towards us.
Step 2: Moving backwards and calling the dog in 🔄
At the moment our dog responds to its name, we briskly start walking backwards – far enough that the dog follows us, comes in our direction and no longer has its original target in focus.

While we keep walking backwards and the dog comes closer and closer, we accompany this with a praising voice and motivating body language. In doing so, we inconspicuously gather in the leash without letting it become taut – after all, the dog is meant to learn to come to us voluntarily.
Step 3: Initiating the “Down” 📍

If we do everything right, our dog follows us for a few steps and we now calmly and completely composedly initiate a “Down” by saying “Down” in a normal voice and bringing the dog into the down position in a relaxed but purposeful way. It must under no circumstances turn away from us.
We achieve this by again moving very slightly backwards while the dog goes into the down, so that the dog glides, so to speak, into the down in our direction.
In unfavourable situations that make a down difficult or even impossible, we can and should replace it with “Sit” for the time being – but only temporarily, until a well-trained “Down” can be used.
Step 4: Waiting and securing ⏱️
As soon as our dog is in the down position, we let calm settle over the situation. If our dog wants to leave the position, we correct it back promptly and quickly.

If our dog is lying securely and calmly, we can call it encouragingly into the sit position. It helps if we take two steps backwards with the command “Sit” – dogs find it easier to get from down into sit this way.
Step 5: Conclusion and reward 🌟
Now we may praise our dog well and reward it with a treat or, even better, with a short, intense game with a toy. Afterwards we continue walking on a long, loose leash.

The training procedure is repeated daily on every suitable walk in the widest variety of situations that arise. The more frequently and the more varied this exercise is carried out, the more deeply the sequences become established in us and the response patterns in the dog.
As a daily training amount, we recommend 20 to 30 repetitions spread across the entire walk on the long leash.
Training progress and integration into daily life 📈

The training takes place while walking and should be integrated into daily routines. We carry the long training leash with us every day and switch to it as soon as we reach suitable terrain away from the road.

Experience shows: If we drop out of long-line training too early and let the dog run off the leash too early, failure is almost guaranteed. Through consistent training, the reward – walking freely with a reliable “Down” in moments of distraction – comes closer and closer over time.

For long-line training: Learning success depends on exercises running with little stress. We therefore strive for a calm and clearly structured training sequence and for the choice of suitable training terrain that is based on the dog’s current level of learning.
Important notes ⚠️
Avoid harsh or loud commands during training and in everyday use.
Avoid tightening the leash.
Avoid carrying out exercises in the direction of the distraction.
Avoid praising too early, while the situation is still ongoing and the dog is restless.
Avoid stress during the procedure.
Avoid the dog leaving the exercise on its own.
Avoid ending the exercise too early, which would lead to the dog breaking out.
Practical impulse: The long-term mission

Pack the training leash every day and use every suitable stretch of path for 20 to 30 relaxed repetitions. Remember: It is not the individual training session that decides, but the sum of calm, positive repetitions over weeks and months. Here, consistency pays off more than any other training measure.
→ Do I stay consistent with long-line training and avoid situations without the long leash?
→ Do I train according to my dog’s level of training and avoid overtaxing it?
→ Do I train daily with the long leash for individual stretches of path?
→ Do I present training with the long leash to my dog as a routine?
→ Do I communicate with my dog calmly and composedly?
→ Did I avoid alarming reactions?
→ Did I address the dog before the leash became taut?
→ Did I walk backwards out of the situation on the long leash until the dog followed me voluntarily?
→ Did I accompany the procedure calmly with praise?
→ Did I lay the dog down into “Down” in a relaxed way?
→ When applying it under real distraction, did I lead the dog far enough out of the situation?
→ Did I let the situation fade away for long enough before I ended and released the exercise?
→ Did I praise calmly and intensively?
